newsitem.title: USA: China may be eyeing more U.S. soybeans - trade.
newsitem.headline: China may be eyeing more U.S. soybeans - trade.

text.p: China may be willing to pay a premium for more soybeans from the United States because of need and availability of shipment, U.S. analysts and exporters said.

"It's feasible. Chinese crushers need prompt shipment of soybeans. One cargo of U.S. soybeans was definitely shipped, but we have no confirmation of additional business," a U.S. oilseed and grain analyst with an international firm said.
Old crop soybean contracts on the Chicago Board of Trade drew support on Tuesday from renewed talk that China was looking to buy U.S. and South American soybeans, traders said.
Demand in China for both soybeans and meal is healthy, according to Hong Kong and China grains traders.

At least one cargo or 1,929,000 bushels of U.S. soybeans was shipped to China for the week ending April 24, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture in its weekly soybean export inspections released Monday.

The U.S. analyst, who spoke on condition of anonymity, noted rumors in world freight markets that China may be interested in possibly one or two additional cargoes of U.S. or Brazilian soybeans for mid-May shipment and in one or two cargoes for June/July, also for optional origin.
But despite the high price, the United States has a chance of getting the business, U.S. exporters said.
"There are several theories. They don't like the coloration of the Paranaguan beans. Fine, but the Chinese are paying an awfully big premium for this stuff," one U.S. exporter said.
For a May position, U.S. No. 2 soybeans at the U.S. Gulf were quoted at $329.10 a tonne FOB while Brazil beans, Paranagua, were $314.05 FOB and Argentinian beans $318.95 FOB.
"I don't think the coloration of beans has anything to do with it. It has to be a time issue," Price Futures Group Vice President Jack Scoville said.

To avoid South American shipping delays, China would turn to the United States. "We can ship quicker than the Brazilians and the Argentinians can," Scoville said. "They pretty much have to come here because the loading schedules are booked. It is like a 28- to 30-day wait in Paranagua port," he said.

Hong Kong and China grains traders on Monday said they could not confirm U.S. soybean sales to China but added that while U.S. beans were more expensive than South American beans, a U.S. deal was not inconceivable.
